entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Lucius Tettius Julianus was a Roman general who held a number of imperial appointments during the Flavian dynasty. Born into a prominent family, Julianus distinguished himself in the military, earning his first legionary command at the age of 21. By 82 CE, he had risen to the rank of legate, overseeing military operations in the eastern provinces. That same year, he was appointed suffect consul for the nundinium of May–June 83, sharing the consulship with Terentius Strabo Erucius Homullus. Julianus's tenure as consul was marked by his efforts to quell the Spartacus Revolt, a major slave uprising that had been brewing in the provinces since 73 CE. Despite the challenges, Julianus successfully crushed the revolt, earning the admiration of Emperor Domitian and securing his position as a key figure in the imperial court. Julianus's legacy extended beyond his military achievements, as he played a significant role in shaping the imperial administration and promoting the interests of the Roman elite. His influence can be seen in the numerous appointments and promotions he secured for his friends and family members, cementing his reputation as a skilled politician and administrator. Tragically, Julianus's life was cut short when he was assassinated in 83 CE, reportedly on the orders of Emperor Domitian.

Through his military campaigns and imperial appointments, Lucius Tettius Julianus left an indelible mark on the Flavian dynasty and the Roman Empire. His legacy serves as a testament to the enduring power of Roman military might and the complexities of imperial politics. Julianus's story also highlights the challenges faced by Roman generals in the 1st century CE, who often found themselves caught between the demands of the emperor, the loyalty of their troops, and the interests of the Roman elite.
